metadata.title: Four Layers, Not One File.
metadata.subtitle: The Claude Config Guide Skill
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: when you ask Claude to change a setting, does the answer come from one settings file, or from something else? Lands the carry-out that Claude's settings live across four layers, not one file, and the guide's routing goes quiet rather than loud if a reference file is missing.

beats.narration_text: Here's what someone assumed: Claude's settings live in a file you can grep. They don't. They live in four layered objects, and the skill is a router, not a database — it picks one of five reference files and opens that. So: which layer holds yours?

beats.narration_text: Here's the actual machinery. Four layers, stacked. Agents sit on top — the actor Claude is playing. Underneath, agent scopes decide how each setting resolves and inherits, field by field, across a workspace. Then identity profiles carry scopes, rules, credentials, and repo permissions, bundled together. And at the bottom: presets, connections, GitHub repos, and custom instructions, each pinned to a profile. The skill file itself is empty of answers — it's an index. Ask a question, it opens one of five reference files: agents and scopes, identity profiles, connections and presets, GitHub and instructions, or best practices.

production_viz.label: FOUR LAYERS, ONE INDEX
production_viz.caption: routes each question to 1 of 5 reference files

beats.narration_text: Five short files instead of one long one — that's the deliberate design choice. They optimized for a reference you can actually load into working memory; they sacrifice the coverage a single monolithic doc would give you. Right now, the guide only speaks to the Slack surface — what changes on desktop or in the API isn't in scope, and the skill won't hedge. And every answer closes the same way: run debug-plugins in a brand-new Slack thread. Fresh thread, fresh container — you see your live configuration, not whatever got cached in the old one.

production_viz.label: SLACK ONLY — VERIFY FRESH
production_viz.caption: new thread = fresh container, not cached state

beats.narration_text: Here's the failure mode. The whole design leans on all five reference files actually being there. Delete one, and the skill goes quiet, not loud — it just won't answer that slice of your question, and nothing surfaces to tell you why. Silent failure is the price of keeping the router simple.
Claude's settings live across four layers, not one file — the guide's whole job is routing you to the right one, and it goes quiet, not loud, if that file is missing.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: I'm designing settings for an app with company-wide defaults, team overrides, and per-user overrides. Walk me through structuring that as layered objects — like agents, scopes, and profiles — so a user's change never gets silently overwritten by a team default. Show a concrete example of the resolution algorithm reading through all three layers. Then name one way the design could quietly fail if a layer file goes missing, and what to add so it fails loud instead. Go deeper: ask the same model to sketch the migration path if you ever need to fold two layers into one — what breaks, what stays, and how you'd A/B test the change without shipping a silent regression.
